### page_1
Palaeomagnetism, rock magnetism and magnetic fabrics in
Precambrian metamorphic terranes of the Huabei Shield, China
J.D.A. Piper a, Zhang Jiasheng b
aGeomagnetism Laboratory, Department of Earth Sciences, University of Liverpool, Liverpool, L69 7ZE, UK
bInstitute of Geology, State Seismological Bureau, P.O. Box 634, 100029 Beijing, China
Received 1 May 1997; accepted 22 September 1998
Abstract
This study has investigated magnetic remanence, rock magnetism and anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) in granulite
and amphibolite grade metamorphic terranes of the Huabei Shield between Inner Mongolia in the west and the Bohai Sea in the
east. Rock magnetic studies identify annealed metamorphic magnetite grains with multidomain properties as the remanence
carriers; a widely recorded stable remanence was probably ﬁxed by grain shape e ects. Granulite facies terranes are typically
between one and two orders more strongly magnetised than amphibolite terranes and AMS fabrics correlate mostly with
metamorphic mineral fabrics observed in the country rocks. Progressive thermal demagnetisation identiﬁes a range of two and
three component structures resident in magnetite. An important component recognised as a partial or complete remagnetisation
by Late Mesozoic–Tertiary tectonic/magmatic activity is present in basement at the southern margin of the outcrop (Miyun
terrane) and where extensive granite plutonism has occurred (Zhunhua terrane). These components have directions
corresponding to remanence in the Yunmeng Shan Granite (119–114 Ma, D/I = 33/58 8, 39 samples, a
95 = 3.58, palaeopole at
2018E, 64 8N). Most remanence elsewhere was probably acquired during post-tectonic uplift and cooling of the basement between
02200 and 1850 Ma because palaeomagnetic directions are removed from the Phanerozoic palaeoﬁeld path and they are distinct
from the palaeomagnetic record in the overlying Jixian Supergroup deposited at 01840–900 Ma. These latter magnetisations are
considered reliable indicators of the palaeoﬁeld during Late Palaeoproterozoic times because deformation of overlying
supracrustal rocks is mostly slight and no prominent deﬂection of magnetic remanence by magnetic fabrics is observed.
Palaeoﬁeld directions and poles attributed to the time of uplift-related cooling are: Qian’an Terrane (D/I = 215/71 8,a
95 =9 8,1 7
samples, pole at 99 8E, 10 8N) and North Qianxi Terrane (D/I = 44/ ÿ 458,a 95 =4 8, 41 samples, pole at 79 8E, 11 8S). In addition,
a more widely-preserved shallow northerly component correlates with a NW 4 E swathe of components recorded by uplift-
related cooling within the Datong–Huan’an granulite terrane in the west of the shield. A preliminary Palaeo-Mesoproterozoic
apparent polar wander path for the Huabei Shield is deﬁned from the Palaeoproterozoic record in the metamorphic basement
rocks and the Meso-Neoproterozoic record in the overlying Jixian Supergroup. It incorporates a loop between 02200 and 1850
Ma and exhibits a general east to west trend in subsequent times. # 1999 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved.
1. Introduction
Although the kinematics of the major Shields during
Precambrian times is quantiﬁed by palaeomagnetic
study, the recoverable record is always incomplete,
both because the rock record is itself only sporadically
preserved, and because later overprinting can obscure
an ancient remanence record. The present Precambrian
palaeomagnetic database is mostly derived from study
of intense, but generally brief, igneous episodes and
platformal successions of Meso- and Neoproterozoic
age. The oldest palaeomagnetic record in each shield is
preserved in the underlying basement rocks. This base-
ment typically comprises a polymetamorphic gneiss
complex produced by crustal accretion and repeated
reworking during Archaean and Early Proterozoic
times.
Whilst metamorphic rocks usually incorporate stable
recorders of ancient remanence and hence provide
scope for extending the palaeomagnetic record of the
Journal of Asian Earth Sciences 17 (1999) 395–419
1367-9120/99/$ - see front matter # 1999 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved.
PII: S 0 7 4 3 - 9 5 4 7 ( 9 8 ) 0 0 0 5 8 - 0

### page_2
shields backwards in time, they have been little stu-
died. The perceived problems include (i) the long time
periods represented by uplift-related cooling, (ii) the
diculty of dating the magnetisations in the absence
of available ﬁeld tests and (iii) the presence of meta-
morphic fabrics which may bias the palaeomagnetic
record in a way which cannot be readily quantiﬁed.
Initial magnetic remanence acquisition in
Palaeoproterozoic metamorphic terranes is generally
linked to the time interval of uplift-related cooling;
this follows the last tectono-thermal episode respon-
sible for reworking the basement and predates depo-
sition of supracrustal successions deposited onto it
(e.g. Morgan, 1976; Piper, 1985, 1992a). In some
examples magnetisation can be speciﬁcally related to
magnetite deposition in microfractures formed during
decompression (Hay et al., 1988; Piper, 1992b). The
remanence is then most obviously linked to age deter-
minations dating isotopic closure in certain meta-
morphic minerals. The diculties with more precise
dating are o set by the ability of these terranes to
record swathes of magnetisations embracing long time
intervals during cooling (Morgan, 1976); they may
then help to constrain whole segments of Proterozoic
apparent polar wander (APW).
Fabrics in metamorphic rocks can be assessed by
measurement of the anisotropy of magnetic suscepti-
bility (AMS) in the palaeomagnetic cores. This is a
bulk parameter recording preferred mineral orientation
by metamorphic crystallisation and/or ﬂow mechan-
isms. The grains contributing to this e ect have para-
magnetic and ferromagnetic properties; the
paramagnetic minerals are mostly the iron-bearing sili-
cates whilst the ferromagnetic contribution is from
magnetite, and sometimes pyrrhotite or hematite. The
strong ferromagnetic e ect of the small volume of
these latter grains is often much larger than the para-
magnetic and (weak negative) diamagnetic e ects of
the bulk silicate matrix. Whilst the inﬂuence of fabric
on the dilute amounts of ferromagnetic grains in
which the stable remanence resides cannot be isolated
by study of AMS, it is a useful qualitative indicator of
bias of magnetic remanence by fabric; a comparison
between results from samples of strong and weak fab-
rics at the same site is often able to recognise the likely
importance of any such bias.
Medium to high grade polymetamorphic terranes
occur along the northern margin of the Huabei (North
China) Shield as inliers exposed beneath supracrustal
successions comprising the Meso-Neoproterozoic
Jixian Supergroup. Cooling of these terranes and their
elevation to present surface levels occurred prior to de-
position of the oldest part of the Jixian succession at
01850 Ma. The remanence must however, have been
acquired after the last stages of ductile deformation
which occurred within the interval 2500–2200 Ma
because regional temperatures were then above the
Curie point. Currently the palaeomagnetism of for-
mations within the Jixian Supergroup provides the
main evidence for Precambrian APW of the Huabei
Shield (Zhang (H.M.) et al., 1991, 1993). In addition
palaeomagnetism and magnetic fabrics in the Datong–
Huai’an granulite region of Inner Mongolia have been
studied by Zhang (J.S.) and Piper (1994) and have
made a preliminary contribution towards deﬁning a
pre-Jixian APW record. This paper reports results
from terranes extending across the northern part of
the shield towards the limit of major exposure north
east of the Bohai Sea (Fig. 1). The collective results
identify aspects of magnetic properties in this
Precambrian basement and contribute towards extend-
ing the APW path of the Huabei shield backwards
into the Palaeoproterozoic era.
2. Geological framework
The Huabei Shield is bounded to the north by the
Mongolian (Central Asian) fold belt and to the south
by the Qilian–Qinling–Dabie Shan. The Tancheng–
Lujiang (Tanlu) fault runs through the eastern part
and cuts the Dabie Shan belt. Although there has been
much debate about the scale of movement on this
fault boundary, no palaeomagnetically-detectable
Fig. 1. Location map and regional outcrop (stippled) of Precambrian metamorphic basement in the North China Shield; see inset for the regional
extent. Area A is the Datong–Huai’an granulite terrane from which palaeomagnetic results are described by Zhang (J.S.) and Piper, 1994). Areas
B and C are the Miyun–Huairou and Zhunhua–Qianxi regions shown in more detail in Figs. 2 and 3.
J.D.A. Piper, Zhang Jiasheng / Journal of Asian Earth Sciences 17 (1998) 395–419396

### page_3
motions between the China and Korean segments are
identiﬁed since Upper Palaeozoic times (Doh and
Piper, 1994). In the Alashan/Hexi Corridor region
linking the Huabei and Tarim Shields, the oldest
exposed rocks belong to the Longshoushan Formation
thought to predate the Luliangian Orogeny at 01850
Ma; these are intruded by 1790 Ma granites (Yang et
al., 1986). As in other parts of the Huabei Shield, little
evidence of volcanism or other signs of instability are
observed in subsequent times suggesting that the cra-
tonic elements were welded together to form a uniﬁed
basement during the Luliangian Orogeny (Ma et al.,
1980).
Geological evidence for Phanerozoic accretion of the
North China Block (incorporating the Huabei Shield)
with Siberia is still controversial and has been assigned
to Middle Palaeozoic (Ren et al., 1987) and Mesozoic
(Klimetz, 1983) times. Palaeomagnetic data suggest a
location along the eastern rim of Gondwana during
Late Precambrian times (Piper and Zhang, 1997). It
had separated from Gondwana by Carboniferous
times and palaeobotanic data imply close proximity to
Eurasia by Upper Carboniferous times (Laveine et al.,
1989). It subsequently moved as a composite block
with Mongolia to become sutured to Siberia in
Mesozoic times (Enkin et al., 1992). Convergence with
the Eastern Asian assembly appears to have taken the
form of anticlockwise rotation about an initial point
of collision near the western end of the South Siberian
Fold Belt (Zhao et al., 1996). Granites generated
during late stages of suturing into the eastern Asian
continental collage were emplaced as plutons into the
metamorphic basement during Cretaceous times; they
constitute the last major thermal event to inﬂuence this
region.
Metamorphic basement of the Huabei Shield is
exposed by uplift of a broad south-facing monocline
and comprises outcrop in four major inliers, namely
the Datong–Huai’an (Fig. 1A), Zhangjiakou–
Xuanhua, Miyun–Huairou (Fig. 1B) and Zhunhua–
Qianxi regions (Fig. 1C). The present paper is con-
cerned mainly with the latter three inliers. Within a ca.
1000200 km area extending from southern Inner
Mongolia in the west to Hebei Province in the east
(Fig. 1) basement outcrop averages some 75–85%
gneisses and 15–25% supracrustal sediments (Qian et
al., 1985). Metamorphism occurred during Archaean
and Early Proterozoic times and the complex deforma-
tional histories are of comparable antiquity. North of
the monocline dips of the Mid-late Proterozoic cover
are mostly less than 10–15 8 and deformation since
uplift has evidently been slight. Block faulting occurred
during Late Mesozoic and Cenozoic times to develop
fractures with a predominant NE–SW orientation;
their locations are partly constrained to ductile shear
belts of Lower Proterozoic age but brittle e ects are
concentrated within a few tens up to a few hundreds
of metres of the fault zones.
The Miyun–Huairou terrane (Fig. 2) comprises pre-
dominant amphibolite facies extensively intruded by
Mesozoic granites; granulite facies rocks are upfaulted
at the east and west sides. Zircon U–Th–Pb and U–Pb
age determinations on the metamorphic rocks are in
the range 2567–2346 Ma (Zhou et al., 1993).
Petrologic studies show that metamorphic conditions
attained temperatures of 650–700 8C in the amphibolite
facies and 800 2 308C at pressures of 8–13.5 kb in the
granulite facies (Lu, 1991).
High grade rocks have a more widespread distri-
bution in the Zhunhua–Qianxi terrane (Fig. 3) where
isotopic data deﬁne basement uplift and deposition of
the ﬁrst cover rocks at 01900 Ma (Sun, 1984). The

morphic terrane. The numbered small black columns are the lo-
cations of the palaeomagnetic sites. The projections show AMS
fabrics deﬁned by directions of maximum (black squares) and inter-
mediate (black triangles) susceptibility plotted as lower hemisphere

### page_4
basement rocks are subdivided here into three groups
comprising:
(i) Granulite facies (the Qianxi Group) locally retro-
gressed to amphibolite facies. The major rock type
is intermediate-acid gneiss derived from a protolith
of tonalite–trondjemite–granodiorite (TTG) anity.
Maﬁc to ultramaﬁc granulites occur as inclusions;
sillimanite–garnet gneisses (khondalites) and some
interbedded supracrustal sediments of banded iron-
stone formation (BIF) are also present.
Temperatures of granulite facies metamorphism
reached 739–1068 8C (Zhang (R.Y.) and Cong,
1981; Wang (R.M.) and Chen, 1982; Wang (R.M.)
et al., 1985; Bai and Yang, 1984; Qian et al., 1985)
at pressures of 11.9–14.2 kb (Zhang (R.Y.) and
Cong, 1981; Qian et al., 1985) or 8–11 kb (Bai and
Yang, 1984) (Fig. 4).
(ii) An amphibolite facies association, composed
mainly of biotite–plagioclase gneisses distributed
Fig. 3. Lithological and sampling site map of the Zhunhua–Qianxi metamorphic terrane (see Fig. 1) with projections of site AMS fabrics.
Symbols are as for Fig. 2.
J.D.A. Piper, Zhang Jiasheng / Journal of Asian Earth Sciences 17 (1998) 395–419398

### page_5
around a high grade core. The metamorphic facies
show transition outwards from high amphibolite
to epidote amphibolite grades and record peak
conditions of 500–760 8C and 6–10 kb (Fig. 4).
(iii) A volcanic-sedimentary succession, metamor-
phosed to lower amphibolite–epidote facies and
distributed along a narrow NNE trending zone in
eastern Qinglong County; an unconformity at the
base is deﬁned by a metamorphosed conglomerate
layer. This succession is a component of an early
Proterozoic orogenic belt at the margin of the cra-
ton formed at 02500 Ma but deformed and meta-
morphosed at 02000–2100 Ma when metamorphic
conditions (see Fig. 4) attained 500–600 8C at 5.5–
7.0 kb in lower amphibolite facies and 05008Ca t
4–6 kb in the epidote-amphibolite facies (Bai and
Yang, 1984).
The igneous protolith at the core of these terranes is
probably of Early-mid Archaean age as deﬁned by age
determinations between 3470–2980 Ma (Jahn et al.,
1987, Liu et al., 1990, 1992). TTG facies within grey
gneisses of the Datong–Huai’an terrane in the west are
of comparable antiquity whilst the Qianxi Group has
yielded 3850–3300 Ma ages (U–Pb zircon results of
Liu et al. (1985, 1992), and Sm–Nd isochron determi-
nations of Jahn and Zhang (1984), Jahn and Ernst
(1990) and Liu et al. (1990). Collectively these studies
identify earliest deposition of supracrustal rocks at
3500–3300 Ma following a crust-forming event.
Age determinations of the granulite facies meta-
morphism are predominantly in the range 2460–2517
Ma (Rb–Sr and Sm–Nd isochron ages, Bai and Yang,
1984; Cui et al., 1989, Jahn et al., 1987; Liu et al.,
1985). Ages derived from the amphibolite facies are
comparable to those from the granulites and in the
range 2450–2650 Ma (Bai and Yang, 1984; Cui et al.,
1989) suggesting that the higher grade amphibolite
facies metamorphism rapidly succeeded granulite facies
in Late Archaean–Early Proterozoic times.
Metamorphism at lower amphibolite to epidote grades
is dated at 2080–2200 Ma (Bai and Yang., 1984)
broadly contemporaneous with polyphase granitoid
intrusion and pegmatite emplacement at around 2200
Ma (Liu et al., 1985; Sun, 1984).
The time sequence of metamorphic conditions, as
summarised in Fig. 4 from data in the Miyun and
Zhunhua–Qianxi regions, deﬁnes a clockwise P-T-t
scheme very similar to that resolved from the Datong–
Huai’an region to the west (Liu et al., 1992, Zhang
(J.S.) and Piper, 1994; Zhang (J.S.) et al., 1994).
Deformation and metamorphic events of the prograde
phase have been largely obliterated by the peak events
which produced tight N–S folds in the Miyun and
Zhunhua–Qianxi regions; later deformation in the
lower grade rocks to the east produced folds with a
NNE trend. The P-T-t trajectory is comparable to
other Precambrian gneiss complexes (Hartley, 1988)
with the clockwise trajectory generally interpreted to
reﬂect crustal thickening during a compressional
phase, possibly in a collisional setting, followed by
extensional collapse.
Temperatures dropped below the Curie points of the
magnetic carriers ( 05808C for magnetite) during

decompression and uplift following the 2100–2200 Ma
events. The metamorphic terranes would subsequently
have cooled to ambient temperatures by the time of
deposition of basal members of the Jixian Supergroup
(01850 Ma) which are unmetamorphosed. Cooling of
the metamorphic rocks through the Curie point there-
fore attributes any primary remanence to the time
interval 02200–1850 Ma.
3. Field and laboratory methods
Cores were drilled at 32 locations in the meta-
morphic rocks, plus igneous intrusions, predating de-
position of the Jixian Supergroup as summarised in
Table 1. In addition the largest member of the
Mesozoic granite-granodiorite suite, the Yunmeng
Shan Granite, was sampled at Site 1 to assess the im-
portance of the Mesozoic thermo-tectonic event in
overprinting the basement rocks. A sampling site com-
prises between seven and twenty two 2.4 cm diameter
cores distributed across at least several metres of out-
crop (e.g. Fig. 7). Cores were oriented in situ by sun
and magnetic compasses and cut into 2.2 cm length
cylinders for magnetic measurements.
Magnetic susceptibilities were initially measured
using a Bartington bridge and AMS fabrics determined
by ‘‘Minisep’’ anisotropy delineator. Cores were then
measured by ‘‘Minispin’’ magnetometers before treat-
ment and following each stage of progressive cleaning
by thermal demagnetisation. The latter employed
Magnetic Measurements demagnetisers in steps of 50
or 100 8C to 500 8C and subsequently in steps of 20 8C
to the Curie points of the magnetic carriers; the

### page_7
ongoing procedure was conducted within a nulliﬁed
ﬁeld environment provided by a large set of Rubens
coils to minimise secondary remanence acquisition.
Components constituting the Natural Remanent
Magnetisation (NRM) in each sample were resolved
by study of orthogonal projections. Characteristic
magnetisations (ChRM’s) were isolated and their
equivalent directions calculated by principal com-
ponent analysis.
3.1. Magnetic properties
A general feature of the intensities of magnetisation
and susceptibilities in Precambrian metamorphic ter-
ranes is a range of several orders of magnitude, con-
trolled by variations in dilute amounts of
ferromagnetic constituents (Tables 1 and 2). This is
also expressed in contrasts between felsic and maﬁc
granulites (Fig. 5a). It is less marked between acid and
basic intrusives; predictably the banded ironstones are
by far the most strongly magnetised facies. The ferro-
magnetic content depends on both the source and the
metamorphic grade. Thus the most important regional
contrast in North China is between the strongly mag-
netised granulite facies terranes and the weakly magne-
tised amphibolite facies rocks of the Qinglong terrane
(Table 1 and Fig. 5b). Although metamorphic rocks in
the latter region are derived mostly from a basic
igneous source, the iron is present in paramagnetic
amphiboles and chlorites, and magnetisations are typi-

oblate (foliated) fabrics on the right from prolate (lineated) fabrics on the left; note that oblate fabrics tend to predominate.

behaviour with J
sf > 10% less than Jsi; a residual tail
is often present indicative of hematite and/or a signiﬁ-
cant contribution of paramagnetic minerals to Js
(Fig. 6a). The BIF have type 3 behaviour in which the
cooling curve crosses the heating curve to give Jsf not
more than 20% higher than Jsi. This e ect is more dif-
ﬁcult to explain but is almost certainly related to beha-
viour of a titanomagnetite mineral; it is possibly due
to a Ti-enriched phase not recognisable on the heating
curve converting to magnetite which has higher Js.
Study of magnetic susceptibility at low temperatures
(KLT analysis) cools the rock to the temperature of
liquid nitrogen ( ÿ1968C) and records susceptibility
during subsequent return to room temperature. The
susceptibility of multi-domain (MD) grains is con-
trolled mainly by magnetocrystalline anisotropy
(Uyeda et al., 1963) which is strongly temperature
dependent: magnetite undergoes a structural change
known as the Verwey transition at ÿ1508C. At this
point the magnetocrystalline anisotropy constant, k1,i s
minimised; a peak in susceptibility near this tempera-
ture is diagnostic of MD magnetite and deﬁnes Group
3 behaviour of Senanayake and McElhinny (1981).
Provided that grain elongation is >10%, single
domain (SD) grain susceptibility is dominated by
shape anisotropy which produces preferential magneti-
sation along the length of an elongate grain to mini-
mise magnetostatic energy (Pullaiah et al., 1975). Since
crystal shapes remain essentially constant with decreas-
Fig. 7. Simpliﬁed illustrations of some sampled outcrops at which more than one site was located. All symbols are the same as for Fig. 2.

area showing a dyke set and sites 27–30. (C) Outcrop from north Qianxi showing the folding of gneiss and site 24. D) Outcrop from Caozhuang
area of western Qian’an showing banded gneiss and site 17 (cores 1–12 from maﬁc granulite lenses, 13–14 from felsic matrix gneiss) and Site 16
(basic dyke).
J.D.A. Piper, Zhang Jiasheng / Journal of Asian Earth Sciences 17 (1998) 395–419 403

### page_10
ing temperature, shape anisotropy is not dependent on
temperature and KLT variations are small.
Superparamagnetic (SP) grains show a susceptibility
falling steadily with temperature due to the increase in
thermal energy. The SD–SP threshold (the ‘‘blocking
volume’’) also decreases with temperature; below
0ÿ 1508C relaxation times of the increasingly-smaller
SP grains extend beyond the period of measurement,
the threshold is then e ectively exceeded and the sus-
ceptibility stabilises (Maher, 1988). Paramagnetic
grains obey the Curie Law and susceptibility falls ex-
ponentially as the temperature rises.
Three parameters used to quantify KLT behaviour
are RS (Relative Susceptibility) = K
ÿ 196/K30,P S
(Peak Susceptibility) = Kpeak/K30 and DS = PS–RS
(Radhakrishnamurty et al., 1977). They give a semi-
quantitative indication of the relative SD and MD
grain contents: DS0 0 corresponds to the presence of
SD grains only whereas DS0 0.9 corresponds to a pre-
dominance of MD grains (Thomas, 1992). Group 3
behaviour is subdivided into 3a and 3b (Table 3) with
the major di erence between the two being that RS is
always less than 0.5 for Group 3a and always greater
than this for Group 3b. Radhakrishnamurty et al.
(1977) describe Group 3a behaviour as indicative of
almost pure MD magnetite with e ectively no Ti sub-
stitution ( x < 0.15); Group 3b behaviour has been con-
sidered to reﬂect the presence of only MD magnetite
(Senanayake and McElhinny, 1981), although
Radhakrishnamurty et al. (1977) consider it to be the
signature of a mixed grain size assemblage with a MD-
dominated assemblage contaminated by small amounts
of SD grains.
Results of KLT analysis are summarised in Table 3
and two curve types are shown in Fig. 6. The granu-
lites exhibit Type 3a behaviour deﬁned by RS mostly
<0.5 indicating a dominance of pure MD magnetite
with no Ti substitution, and group 3b behaviour indi-
cating a mixed grain size of magnetite but with MD
grains still dominating over SD grains (Thomas, 1992).
The banded ironstones also exhibit dominant MD
behaviour (Table 3). The amphibolites either show
type 2 curves (Senanayake and McElhinny, 1981) indi-
cating that paramagnetic minerals dominate the KLT
expression, or have hybrid type 2/3 curves with detect-
able MD magnetite.
High temperature susceptibility (KHT) analysis ob-
serves the variation in magnetic susceptibility when
samples are heated to temperatures above the Curie
point. Dominant MD behaviour is characterised by a
broad Hopkinson peak yielding the H curve type of
Radhakrishnamurty and Likhite (1970). Grains with
SD behaviour at room temperature convert to SP
behaviour at higher temperatures so that the suscepti-
bility peaks before dropping gradually to the Curie
point; this kind of curve is therefore the signature of
dominant SD grain properties. The same e ect is pro-
duced by a decrease in Ti content of the magnetite and
the maximum susceptibility is attained at progressively
higher temperatures as Ti is reduced (Dunlop, 1974;
Appel and So el, 1985). Domain structure is sensitive
to temperature changes and it is also common to ﬁnd
that irreversible changes take place such that a SD
heating curve converts to an H type (MD) curve on
cooling; this is referred to a quasi-single domain
(QSD) type behaviour. The granulites and BIF facies
exhibit H type behaviour (Fig. 6c) with small amounts
of alteration during heating. KHT results thus re-
inforce the results of KLT analysis to show magnetic
grains are dominated by MD grain assemblages. The
response of the amphibolites to KHT analysis was too
weak to quantify (Table 3).
Magnetic hysteresis was determined by subjecting
samples to a cycled magnetic ﬁeld within a vibrating
sample magnetometer. The form of the hysteresis
curve is expressed by the magnetisation at saturation
(M
s), the residual magnetisation when the applied ﬁeld
is reduced to zero ( Mrs), and the back ﬁeld required to
reduce this saturation to zero (this is the coercive
force, H
c). If Mrs00 the result is a straight line of
positive slope (i.e. there is no hysteresis), magnetisation
is proportional to applied ﬁeld and the behaviour is
essentially paramagnetic. M
s and Mrs are dependent
on the concentration and type of the magnetic min-
erals present; Ms is independent of grain size but Mrs
is smaller for MD than for SD grain properties. Hence
the ratio of Mrs/Ms is a useful indicator of domain
states: if Mrs/Ms < 0.1 the sample is dominated by
MD grains, if Mrs/Ms > 0.1 small but signiﬁcant frac-
tions of SD grains are indicated within a dominant
MD assemblage. Provided that these mixed domain
sizes are present within magnetite only (indicated by
M
rs/Ms values of 0.02–0.5), the equation:
XMD 0:5ÿ Mrs=Ms=0:48
yields an estimate of the fraction of MD grains present
(Thomas, 1992) (Table 3).
The results of hysteresis analysis (Table 3) show that
the granulites in the Huabei Shield have saturation
magnetisations an order or more stronger than the
amphibolite facies. A saturation achieved in low
applied ﬁelds and the M
rs/Ms values indicate that mag-
netite is the mineral responsible for hysteresis in the
granulites; the XMD ratios identify a predominant MD
character to these grains. In contrast, a barely percep-
tible hysteresis in samples from the amphibolite facies
indicate that paramagnetic minerals dominate the mag-
netic response here.
Thus the rock magnetic tests show that pure magne-
tite grains with annealed properties stable to heating
are responsible for the ferromagnetism of the granu-
J.D.A. Piper, Zhang Jiasheng / Journal of Asian Earth Sciences 17 (1998) 395–419404

### page_11
lites. KLT, KHT and hysteresis studies all support the
conclusion that the magnetite grain structure is predo-
minantly or entirely MD. Thus the stable magnetic
behaviour of these rocks (Section 5) indicates that
either only a small fraction of the ﬁner grain sizes con-
tribute to the remanence in this facies, or (more prob-
ably) that domain walls in MD grains are pinned by
e ects such as grain shape. The signiﬁcance of grain
shape is implied by the reports of blade and needle-
like grain forms in these facies elsewhere (e.g. Morgan
and Smith, 1981; Piper, 1987; Zhang (J.S.) and Piper,
1994).

Most samples have dual component remanence
structure with a low blocking temperature (lbt) com-

treatment (100 8C) and a second more distributed com-
ponent removed by 500 8C. These ChRM’s have

with a few components veering towards a more east-

the mean declination is directed NE whilst the incli-
nation is close to the present geomagnetic ﬁeld incli-
nation (+60 8) at this latitude (Table 4a and 4b).
Sites 2 (dyke) and 3 (granulite) are in the metamor-
phosed country rock within 10 km of the granite mar-
gin and within its probable thermal inﬂuence. The
dyke has AMS foliation subparallel to the dyke plane
and horizontal k
1, whilst the magnetic foliation in the
granulite is in the plane of the gneissosity (Fig. 2).
Thermal overprinting by the granite is indicated by a
dominance of NE + ChRM’s (e.g. samples 2–5 and 3–
9 in Fig. 8c).
The Yunmeng Shan pluton is located within the
monoclinal limb at the southern margin of meta-
morphic basement outcrop in the Huabei Shield. It has
been emplaced in the footwall of the Hefangkou Fault
and exposed by core complex uplift during extensional
tectonism (Davis et al., 1996). The sampled part lies
below a (Shuiyu) mylonitic shear zone which deﬁnes
the roof of the core complex and dips at 0208 south
eastwards. The AMS fabric does not record this shear
zone; instead the k
1ÿ k2 AMS plane dips at a shallow
angle towards the SW and is evident in the easterly
dip of k3 normals to this plane (Fig. 8a). Comparable
fabric orientations are recorded in the granite along
the border of the pluton (Davis et al. 1996). It is poss-
ible that this fabric is related to primary magmatic
ﬂow; on the assumption that the k
1ÿ k2 plane was
horizontal at the time of cooling of the granite body,
the remanence direction adjusted for dip is D/I = 25.2/
67.28 which yields a pole position at 170.6 8E, 70.1 8N
plotting on the China APW path between 150 and 100
Ma (Fig. 14) and compatible with the 119–114 Ma
radiometric age. Consideration of the remanence with-
out tilt adjustment would make no essential di erence
to this interpretation; movements of the body during
emplacement to the present level are more dicult to
evaluate: whilst it is likely that the entire region has
undergone some rotation about a near-horizontal axis
during footwall uplift, any simple rotation of the gran-

Partial recovery of magnetisations unrelated to the
granite is evident at greater distance from the contact:
sites 4 and 5 include ChRM’s with more northerly

Ironstones of Site 7 have discrete magnetisations
which, although not subtracted until the Curie point
of magnetite (Sample 7-2 in Fig. 9), are so close to the
mean geomagnetic ﬁeld (D/I = 0/ + 60 8) that they can-

The contact with a nearby rapakivi-type intrusion has
similar declination but shallower inclination in narrow
to distributed blocking temperature spectra (Samples

fabric (Fig. 2). A Mesoproterozoic volcanic suite
spatially and temporally associated with rapakivi gran-
ite intrusions, including the sampled (Shachang) body,
is linked to a mid-Proterozoic extensional tectonic
regime (Yu et al., 1994). Age determinations on this
intrusion are 1715 Ma (zircon U–Pb), 1588 Ma (biotite
K–Ar) and 1311 Ma (Rb–Sr, Yu et al., 1994).
Sites 8 to 15 are in basic lavas, dykes and sheets
(Table 1) from the Qinglong terrane in the eastern part

of the Zhunhua–Qianxi inlier (Fig. 1) and assigned to

they comprise the highest crustal level investigated

amphibolite facies in the west to epidote to low amphi-
bolite grade in the east and primary structures are
widely preserved. The investigated section comprises a
traverse from near the contact with a member of the
Mesozoic granite suite outwards into country rock
remote from younger magmatism (Fig. 3). Sites far
from the granite tend to show Recent ﬁeld components
removed by 300 8C to recover a N–NNE remanence of
shallower positive inclination (Samples 10-2, 11-7 in
Fig. 10); a few examples of opposite polarity occur

contact are close to in situ remanence in the Yunmeng
Shan Granite (Table 4, Fig. 8b and 14); elsewhere
ChRM’s have contrasting declinations and tend to
have shallower inclination. Application of a palaeo-
magnetic fold test (McFadden, 1990) to the ﬁve stable
sites (8, 10, 11, 13 and 154) shows that the hypothesis
assuming a magnetisation acquired before deformation

tisations in the amphibolites postdate deformation and
(with the exception of sites 10 and 13, Table 4) cannot
be distinguished from the Mesozoic ﬁeld.
AMS in the amphibolitised volcanics is dominated
by foliatated fabrics with k1ÿ k2 planes dipping to the
north west (Fig. 3). This is approximately orthogonal
to the regional ESE dip of the succession and con-
forms to metamorphic foliation measured at outcrop.
Close to the granite contact dip of the AMS foliation
in dyke (Site 9) and host lavas (Site 8) changes to SE
or is composite (Site 15, Fig. 3) and appears to be
inﬂuenced by proximity to granite emplacement.

AMS fabrics within the Qian’an terrane are complex
and appear to reﬂect deformation: at least two AMS
foliation planes are present in the strongly deformed
granulites at the Yugou iron mine (Site 19, Fig. 3).
Site 16 retains a primary foliation near to the plane of
the dyke whilst host granulites (Site 17) have foliation
dipping steeply to the west in the basic lenses and to
the east in the acid granulites (Fig. 7D). This is prob-
ably an example where the quartz-bearing felsic
gneisses acted as a ‘‘softer’’ matrix and experienced
stronger ductile deformation. The key observation is
that the k
1 directions of these fabrics show no obvious
relationship to the northerly shallow magnetic rema-
nence that characterises these rocks; at Site 17 it is
nearly orthogonal. Thus we suspect no strong inﬂuence
of magnetic fabric on remanence here.
Samples of the basement terrane north-east of the
town of Qianxi comprise basic and felsic granulites
(represented by Sites 20–24 and 26) and a cross cutting
basic dyke (Sites 25). The antiquity of the granulite
protolith in this region is indicated by 03500 Ma ages
(Liu et al., 1990). The dominant feature of magnetic
remanence is a NE-magnetisation (Samples 23-2 and
24-1 in Fig. 12) although declinations can range from
northerly to easterly (Samples 23-4 and 22-2 in Fig. 12
and see Fig. 13). Some antiparallel lower blocking tem-
perature components suggest a dipolar record and a
dual polarity structure is present in some single cores
(Samples 20-8 and 24-5 respectively in Fig. 12).
AMS fabrics in the North Qianxi terrane have vari-
able orientations which mostly correspond to tectonic
fabrics observed at outcrop. Di erences are again
recorded within individual sites at 20 and 22–24
between the AMS foliations in basic lenses and the fel-
sic host (Fig. 3). Maximum susceptibility directions are
unrelated to the dominant NE-magnetic remanence.
The remaining sites in the western part of this inlier
occur north of Zhunhua (Sites 27–33, Fig. 3) and are
in a sector invaded by numerous small granite plutons
of Mesozoic age. Partial overprinted contributions of
the Mesozoic to Recent ﬁeld are present as lower
blocking temperature components in acid and basic
dykes at Sites 27–30 (eg. Samples 27-1 and 30-2 in
Fig. 11) whilst possible ChRM’s of more ancient origin
have directions which are steeper (e.g Samples 27-5
and 30-2 in Fig. 11). At Sites 31–33 some ChRM decli-
nations are more easterly (e.g. Samples 31-7, 32-2 and
33-1 in Fig. 11). The dyke at Site 33 has been meta-
morphosed with country rock of Site 32 and the domi-
nant NE+ ChRM therefore records a common
overprint. Sites 31–33 lie near the northern extremity
of the basement inlier and dip northwards beneath the
sub-Jixian unconformity. Although providing no sig-
niﬁcant test ( }
tilt adjusted = 1.049, } = 3.086 for N = 7),
adjustment of the steep ChRM’s at these sites for tilt
moves their ChRM’s closer to the shallower ChRM’s
at the remaining Sites 27–30 (Table 4) and suggests
that basement and cover may have been folded since
acquisition.
Sites 27–30 from the same outcrop are deformed
and sheared at the margins but preserve a post-tectonic
AMS fabric contrasting with gently dipping meta-
morphic foliation in the country rocks at this location
(Fig. 7B). Thus bodies 27–29 have steep foliation
planes aligned close to the dyke planes whilst basic
granulite lenses in gneisses of site 31 have weak mag-
netic fabrics correlating with metamorphic foliation
(Fig. 3). Site 33 is an example of a composite fabric
with one AMS foliation close to the dyke plane.
5. Regional magnetisations and pole positions
The magnetisation in medium-high grade basement
terranes is always post-tectonic. The earliest opportu-
nity for remanence acquisition occurs during post-oro-
genic collapse and cooling below the Curie point
isotherm ( 05808C for magnetite). Since the processes
of remanence acquisition are very prolonged, even
rock volumes as small as an individual core will have
averaged short term variations of the magnetic ﬁeld
such as secular variation; this prolonged acquisition is
enhanced by the lowering and broadening of the
blocking temperature spectra consequent upon slow
cooling (Pullaiah et al., 1975). Sample ChRM magneti-
sations are then integrated e ects yielding palaeomag-
netic poles; this is sometimes evident from recovery of
a dual polarity structure during the demagnetisation of
single cores. It can also mean that a varied remanence
record is often recovered within a single palaeomag-
netic site: local di erences in magnetic mineralogy can
result in remanence acquisition over time periods sep-
arated by many millions of years. Orthogonal plots
from nearby cores shown in Figs. 9–12 illustrate this
facet of basement magnetisation.
Accordingly no detailed analysis of data at site level
is merited. Instead the populations of ChRM com-
ponents form the basis of palaeomagnetic interpret-
ation and are summarised as terrane by terrane
distributions in Fig. 13. The distribution of sample

### page_20
magnetisations in the Datong–Huan’ai terrane to the
west of the study region (Zhang (Q.R.) and Piper,
1994) is also shown in Fig. 13 and is a typical record
from a granulite basement. It identiﬁes a long swathe
of dual polarity magnetisations with northerly and
southerly-directions of shallow inclination. The
remaining record is observed to change along the
Huabei Shield: although N–S shallow directions are
sporadically developed, and may have recorded the
same interval of uplift-related cooling as that identiﬁed
in the Datong–Huai’an terrane, this is no longer the
dominant feature of the distributions to the east
(Fig. 13).
Since palaeomagnetic ﬁeld tests are typically una-
vailable in basement terranes, interpretation of these
magnetisations must have recourse to comparison with
the established APW path of the North China Block.

### page_21
made in Fig. 14 and with the post-metamorphic
Proterozoic record in Fig. 15 and Table 5. Although
post-uplift tilting of these rocks cannot be determined
in the interior of the terranes, the Mesoproterozoic
cover surrounding the metamorphic inliers has low
dips seldom exceeding 10–15 8. It is therefore unlikely
that the basement rocks have been appreciably tilted
since uplift to surface levels and in situ consideration
of the palaeomagnetic directions and pole positions is
associated with only minor uncertainties.
Magnetisations in granulites of the East Miyun
Terrane have NE+ directions at Site 5 and part of
Site 4; these are typically steeper than the Mesozoic–
Recent ﬁeld and yield pole MY1 removed from the
Phanerozoic path (Fig. 14). The Shachang rapakivi
intrusion has shallower inclination remanence (pole
MY2) of possible Mesoproterozoic age. The remaining
N+ magnetisations recognised in granulites at Sites 4
and 6, and ironstones of Site 7, have directions which
cannot be distinguished from much younger ﬁeld direc-
tions (Table 4); it is therefore unclear whether pole
MY3 records a Mesozoic–Recent overprint or a pri-
mary magnetisation fortuitously near to the present
ﬁeld (Fig. 14).
With the exception of Sites 11(b) and 13 (Table 4),
magnetisations in the Qinglong amphibolite terrane
are northerly but mostly shallower than the Recent
ﬁeld. The pole AM1 is post-deformational and could
also possibly be a Mesozoic overprint (Fig. 14). The
Qian’an terrane has two ChRM populations compris-
ing a steep positive magnetisation yielding pole QN2
and a shallow northerly magnetisation yielding pole
QN1. The latter falls within the swathe of magnetisa-
tions observed in the Datong–Huai’an granulite ter-
rane (Fig. 13) which is a basement outcrop devoid of
Mesozoic magmatism and where Mesoproterozoic dyk-
ing is apparently the last thermal inﬂuence. Since it
also contrasts with much of the Meso- and
Neoproterozoic Jixian record, this swathe is probably
a primary uplift and cooling-related acquisition at
02100 Ma. This is also our preferred interpretation of
pole QN1.

The poles are coded as in Table 4. Mean palaeomagnetic poles embracing the swathe of components resolved from the Datong–Huai’an terrane
(Zhang (J.S.) and Piper, 1994) are shown as the tied black squares. The Phanerozoic apparent polar wander path from the North China Block as
deﬁned by mean poles of Zhao et al. (1996) is shown for comparison and links mean poles for Carboniferous (C), Early and Late Permian (P1,
P2), Early and Late Triassic (T1, T3), Early and Late Jurassic (J1 and J3), Early and Late Cretaceous (K1, K2) and Tertiary (T) times.
J.D.A. Piper, Zhang Jiasheng / Journal of Asian Earth Sciences 17 (1998) 395–419 415

### page_22
To the north in the granulite terrane of North East
Qianxi characteristic magnetisations are predominantly
NE. This record cannot be confused with the
Phanerozoic ﬁeld, and yields palaeopole QX2 plotting
at the eastern extremity of Meso- and Neoproterozoic
poles; hence we conclude that it is primary, and
acquired during a stage of the uplift-related cooling.
As is typical of this kind of imprint, it appears to
record a swathe of declinations (Fig. 13), and probably
a segment of APW, although the limited sample only
merits a single group mean calculation. Minor popu-
lations of NW shallow components (yielding pole
QX1) and steep positive components (yielding pole
QX3) are also present. The former corresponds to the
western extension of the swathe of magnetisation in
the Datong–Huai’an terrane granulites (Zhang (J.S.)
and Piper, 1994) and could be a primary magnetisa-
tion. However, it is also observed that this part of the
swathe is close to the Upper Palaeozoic APW path
(Fig. 14). No widespread Permian overprinting appears
to be recorded in North China (Zhao et al., 1996)
although Triassic overprinting (cf. mean poles T1 and
T3 in Fig. 14) is widely identiﬁed further south in the
vicinity of the Qinling Belt formed by welding of the
North and South China Blocks (Kent et al., 1987;
Wang (R.M.) and Van der Voo, 1993; Zhao et al.,
1996, Zhang (Q.R.) and Piper, 1997).
The northerly positive magnetisation (mean D/
I = 19/598) is the exclusive feature of the North
Zhunhua Terrane (Fig. 13). Although there is some in-
dication that the northern margin of the basement has
been folded since acquisition, this could have occurred
during core complex uplift, and the pole ZH1 is indis-
tinguishable from the Late Mesosoic ﬁeld (Fig. 14).
We therefore consider that it is probably a regional
overprint acquired during the extensive Cretaceous
plutonic igneous activity in this region (Fig. 3).
The fabrics recorded by AMS have their origins in
mineral growth within a ductile regime under a re-
gional stress ﬁeld, as well as by subsequent microfrac-
ture inﬁlling (Zhang (J.S.) and Piper, 1984). Magnetic
remanence is typically a later feature acquired over a
broad blocking temperature spectrum commencing at
a temperature somewhat below the laboratory Curie
points of the ferromagnetic carriers. Hence primary
remanence acquisition by thermal or thermo-chemical
Fig. 15. Pole positions of inferred Proterozoic age from the North China Shield. An apparent polar wander path is proposed to embrace the
time sequence of poles incorporating two loops (see Section 7). The poles are summarised and coded as in Table 5. Poles MY3 and ZH1 from
this study are excluded as possible Mesozoic–Recent overprints (see text).
J.D.A. Piper, Zhang Jiasheng / Journal of Asian Earth Sciences 17 (1998) 395–419416

### page_23
processes to impart a TRM or TCRM corresponds
with the last part of the P-T-t loop in Fig. 4 and corre-
lates with regional post-metamorphic uplift dated
02100–1850 Ma in this region (Section 2). The magne-
tisations yielding pole QN1, QN2, QX1 and QX2 from
the Qian’an and NE Qianxi terranes which do not cor-
relate with known younger palaeomagnetic directions
are considered to record palaeoﬁelds from this time
period. The remaining record is indistinguishable from
later ﬁeld directions and cannot therefore be conﬁ-
dently assigned to the interval of uplift-related cooling.
Indeed there is strong indication that much of this
magnetisation record is a Late Mesozoic overprint
acquired during emplacement of the North China
Block into the eastern Asian collage and ensuing mag-
matism; this is most notably the case in the Miyun and
North Zhynhua terranes (poles MY3 and ZH1) where
poles are close to the Late Cretaceous APW path for
North China and where granite emplacement of this
age is extensive. We are unable to draw a speciﬁc link
with the result from the Yunmeng Shan granite owing
to uncertainties about its orientation during magnetisa-
tion (Section 3). Overprinting of early Mesozoic age is
a possible explanation of magnetisations in the low
grade metamorphic terrane at Qinglong (pole AM1).
6. Proterozoic apparent polar wander of the Huabei
Shield
Inspection of Figs. 2, 3, 7 and 13 identiﬁes no
obvious bias of magnetic remanence by AMS linea-
tion; also (and in contrast to the Datong–Huai’an ter-
rane, see Zhang (J.S.) and Piper, 1994) we ﬁnd no
signiﬁcant tendency for the swathes of component
directions to lie within the planes of foliation. Hence
we infer that fabrics in these metamorphic rocks have
not deﬂected the remanence in a major way although
some e ect will no doubt be present. Dunlop and
O¨zdemir (1997) summarise present evidence relating
anisotropy to deﬂection of remanence; observational
evidence is variable, but in theory, a susceptibility ani-
sotropy of 22% (equivalent to the higher range of
AMS values observed in this study) is equivalent to a
maximum deﬂection of the remanence of 11.6 8; this
would inﬂuence only in detail the rather general con-
clusions that can be drawn from the remanence record
in metamorphic terranes. The implication is that the
pole positions derived from primary magnetisations in
the metamorphic basement can be reliably used to de-
ﬁne APW during the interval of uplift-related cooling.
The palaeomagnetic database from the Huabei
Shield is summarised in Table 5. This compilation
excludes earlier and poorly documented data but in-
corporates the studies based on modern methods of
demagnetisation and component analysis (Zhang
(H.M.), 1995a). The bulk of the Meso- and
Neoproterozoic results are derived from formations of
the Jixian Supergroup (Zhang (H.M.) et al., 1991;
Zhang (H.M.), 1995b). The remaining data are from
the metamorphic basement rocks (Liu et al., 1984;
Zhang (J.S.) and Piper, 1994 and this study) and
Meso-Proterozoic dykes (Qian and Chen 1987; Zhang
(J.S.) and Piper, 1994).
Few of the studies summarised in Table 5 have as-
sociated palaeomagnetic ﬁeld tests and most of the
Jixian results are from single locations or small num-
bers of sites; assignment of ages to these magnetisa-
tions from sedimentary rocks is fraught with
uncertainty. However, the bulk of the Jixian poles plot
in the central Paciﬁc region between 200 and 270 8E
and north of, or close to, the equator. The current
basis for regarding this as a record of Meso-
Neoproterozoic APW is a distinction between these
data and the Carboniferous and later APW path, and
speciﬁcally an absence of overprinting by the Late
Mesozoic magmatic activity.
The bulk of the Proterozoic ( 02200–900 Ma) poles
from China plot as a distribution running across the
north west Paciﬁc and occupying a swathe which is ap-
proximately equatorial with respect to the North
China Shield (Fig. 15). The limit of this distribution at
poles QX1 and DHA4 overlaps with the Phanerozoic
path and could therefore be inﬂuenced by later remag-
netisation; the remainder of the swathe coincides with
no known Phanerozoic data and can therefore be
interpreted with some conﬁdence as a Proterozoic
record. These poles embrace a very long interval of
geological time and, since their age control is broad, it
may be premature to use them to deﬁne the shape of
the APW path. However, there are several indications
that at least two loops of comparable form are
recorded here: ﬁrstly, poles from probable primary
magnetisations in the metamorphic basement (NS,
STF, QN2, QX2, NZF, and QX3) plot to the east of
all the Jixian supracrustal data with the exception of
two results from the Mesoproterozoic Dahongyu
Formation (Fig. 15). Hence we recognise a general
east to west APW motion between Palaeo- and
Mesoproterozoic times. In the context of the uplift his-
tory of the North China Shield (Section 2), we suspect
that the age of the older poles is somewhat younger
that the lower limit of 2300 Ma given by Liu et al.
(1984).
Secondly, the other key component of the
Palaeoproterozoic record in the Huabei Shield is the
Datong–Huai’an swathe (mean poles coded DHA in
Fig. 15 and dated 02100 Ma) which also includes pole
QN1 and possibly pole QX1. The sense of motion
along this swathe is not known for certain although
Zhang (J.S.) and Piper (1994) suggest that it was from
DHA14 DHA4. These data are therefore shown in
J.D.A. Piper, Zhang Jiasheng / Journal of Asian Earth Sciences 17 (1998) 395–419 417

### page_24
Fig. 15 as a loop commencing with the other
Palaeoproterozoic poles QN2, STF, NS and QX2 and
returning via probable Mesoproterozoic poles from the
oldest of the supracrustal rocks with assigned ages of
01850 Ma (XF1, XF2, CF, DG, CHD1); poles MY2
and AM1 could fall on the return segment of this
track or (as noted above) record Mesozoic overprint-
ing. It also remains possible that the Palaeoproterozoic
segment of this loop has the opposite trend commen-
cing with the Datong–Huai’an swathe and moving
towards the poles QX2, QN2, STF and NS.
Palaeopoles from the oldest of the Mesoproterozoic
cover rocks (MF, XF1, XF2, CF, DG and CHD1) are
dispersed and suggest the possibility of appreciable
APW motion during these times. It is possible that
subsequent APW was rather low however, because
younger Mesoproterozoic formations of the Jixian
Supergroup (01700–1300 Ma) are distributed along an
east to west trend of little more than 50 8 (poles TF,
DR1, GF1, GF2, GF3, YF1, YF2 and WR2).
Although it is not yet deﬁned with clarity, a loop is
then required to embrace poles from late
Mesoproterozoic dyke swarms emplaced into the cold
shield (poles BI, NSD and NWD in Fig. 15). Poles
from Neoproterozoic formations of the Jixian
Supergroup and elsewhere plot further to the west of
the Meso- and Palaeoproterozoic poles and reﬂect a
trend also seen in APW paths from other shields such
as Laurentia and Baltica (Piper, 1987).
Thus the Precambrian palaeomagnetic record from
the North China Shield appears to commence at about
2200 Ma and deﬁne a general east to west trend
through more than 1200 Ma of Proterozoic times. We
propose that at least two APW loops are incorporated
within this general trend, although more well-dated
magnetisations are required to deﬁne these (and poss-
ible other loops) more clearly.
